title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale–State Feedback GovernsRecurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs

paper.title: When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale–State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs
paper.abstract:
Abstract Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that
state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at
every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that
leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state
it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion
entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are
separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware
scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under
article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few
layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more
than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the
decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Suppose you quantize the recurrent state of a linear-attention model to INT4 and check it the usual way, with needle-in-a-haystack retrieval. Recall comes back perfect at every length you measure, so you ship it. Past the longest length you tested, the best of the four-bit policies still recovers the planted needle on demand, and its perplexity on ordinary text has risen eightfold. It remembers the fact and has stopped being a language model. Both halves of that story are measured below, and both are invisible to the way recurrent-state quantization is currently reported. Linear-attention and state-space models replace the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state : Gated DeltaNet (GDN) powers the linear layers of Qwen3-Next ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) , Kimi Linear ( Kimi Team, 2025 ) builds on it, and Mamba-2 is a widely used SSM. That state is a real deployment cost during long decode, so quantizing it is the natural remedy. But a recurrent state is not a weight tensor. It is rewritten at every decode step , so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound, and a bit-width certified as safe at short exposure need not stay safe as decode proceeds . Per-token dynamic INT4 leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at H = 0 H=0 and destroys it by H = 1024 H=1024 (Figure 1 a). Three things have kept that axis out of view. The closest developed literature is low-bit KV-cache quantization ( Hooper et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , where the cache is stored rather than recurrent, so error never re-enters the state and exposure is not reported as a variable. Quantization research more broadly grew up on weights and activations ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ; Frantar et al., 2023 ) , neither of which carries its own quantization error into the next step. And the probe everyone reaches for is retrieval accuracy, which turns out to be the least sensitive instrument available for this failure. The eightfold rise in the opening paragraph is what that insensitivity costs, and a warning in its own right. Figure 1: The phenomenon. (a) NIAH recall over 12 seeds against quantized decode horizon H H . Every bit-width is intact at H = 0 H=0 and decays as the state is overwritten; INT5 traces the frontier. (b) Mean recurrent-state norm on independent articles, log scale: per-token dynamic INT4 inflates it by two to three orders of magnitude, while the static curves and the unquantized reference coincide along the bottom. Nothing is measured between H = 0 H=0 and H = 1024 H=1024 , so that span is dotted; 2B was not run at H = 8192 H=8192 . Prior work quantizes these caches with architecture-specific machinery: Q-Mamba ( Chen et al., 2025 ) reaches an INT4 Mamba-2 state cache via trained DSQ/ESR alongside weights and activations, and the Nemotron 3 line ships FP16 with stochastic rounding for the Mamba SSM cache ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) . We instead study state-only, training-free fake-quantization , to isolate what the recurrence does to quantization error independently of any trained corrector. We contribute: • A failure frontier in (bit-width × \times decode horizon), making decode horizon an explicit stability axis for recurrent-cache quantization (§ 4 ). • A scale–state feedback mechanism for per-token dynamic scaling, causally identified by a scale-yoking intervention that removes the numerical runaway but only part of the functional loss, and a unifying account of containment that explains why a calibrated ceiling, periodic reset and persistent scaling all work, and why which of them works best depends on the architecture (§ 5 , § 6 ). • A universal policy × \times exposure interaction with a model-dependent short-horizon reversal, replicated on independent articles across architectures and scales (§ 7 ). • A negative result : every outlier-locating allocation loses to plain group-wise scaling, while per-layer allocation helps only to collapse onto a trivial rule (§ 8 ), and a survival analysis showing that short evaluations certify policies as safe long before their failures appear (§ 9 ).

sections.heading: Linear-attention and state-space LLMs.
sections.text: Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a kernel-feature recurrence and a fixed-size state ( Katharopoulos et al., 2020 ) ; the delta rule sharpens that recurrence ( Schlag et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) , and Gated DeltaNet ( Yang et al., 2025 ) is the linear component of Qwen3-Next ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) , while Kimi Linear ( Kimi Team, 2025 ) extends it with finer-grained gating. State-space models ( Gu and Dao, 2024 ; Dao and Gu, 2024 ) carry context in an SSM state. All of them share the property we study: a fixed-size recurrent state, overwritten each step.

sections.heading: Cache quantization.
sections.text: For softmax attention the analogous target is the growing KV cache, and low-bit KV-cache quantization is well developed ( Hooper et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . The recurrent case differs: the cache is constant-size but recurrent , so each step’s error enters the state that produces the next one. Beyond Q-Mamba ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , Quamba2 ( Chiang et al., 2025 ) quantizes Mamba weights and activations (W8A8 through W4A16) together with the inputs of the linear recurrence, MambaQuant ( Xu et al., 2025 ) applies variance-aligning rotations to weights and activations, and ReplaySSM ( Dao, 2026 ) recomputes state from cached inputs rather than quantizing it at all. Of these only Q-Mamba reaches the persistent state, and only alongside weights and activations. Concurrent work DAMP ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) quantizes the GDN and KDA state directly, choosing high-risk channels offline by quantization-error energy and decay persistence. It runs at about 9.9 bits per state value on 35B and 48B models, with deployment kernels, and reports that INT4 and NVFP4 collapse accuracy. We hold everything else in full precision, work below five bits, and vary how long the state is quantized, an axis DAMP holds fixed. Kozyrev and Maiboroda (2026) instead quantize weights and activations of a hybrid 27B model and find injected noise flat over 32K tokens. There the stored state stays in high precision, so the scale never becomes a function of the corrupted state.

sections.heading: Outliers and group-wise quantization.
sections.text: A large body of LLM-quantization work targets activation outliers—mixed-precision on outlier channels ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , migrating outlier scale into weights ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , second-order error compensation ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) , and activation-aware protection of salient weights ( Lin et al., 2024 ) —and group-wise scaling is a standard remedy. Locating the outlier channels does not beat uniform group-wise quantization, because the recurrent failure is a scale–state feedback to be contained rather than a static set of outliers to be handled. Sensitivity-aware mixed precision is likewise well established, from Hessian-trace layer allocation ( Dong et al., 2020 ) to layer-wise KV precision search ( Li et al., 2025 ) and per-head rate-distortion allocation ( Zuo et al., 2026 ) . Our leak-free audit (§ 8 ) shows this machinery is unnecessary here: sensitivity is so concentrated in the first layers that a learned allocator, a knapsack optimizer, and a trivial protect-first-few-layers baseline coincide.

sections.heading: Models.
sections.text: Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B (official Gated DeltaNet hybrid ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Qwen Team, 2026 ) , 262K context, BF16 compute with FP32 recurrent state) and Mamba-2-1.3B ( Dao and Gu, 2024 ) ( state-spaces , native loader). The GDN recurrent state has shape ( 1 , 16 , 128 , 128 ) (1,16,128,128) ; the Mamba SSM state ( 1 , 64 , 64 , 128 ) (1,64,64,128) .

sections.heading: Quantization.
sections.text: We apply symmetric per-channel INT- b b fake-quantization to the recurrent state at each decode step: round, clamp, dequantize. Scaling at channel or vector granularity is the standard response to activation outliers ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ) , and group-wise scaling the one KV-cache quantizers use ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Hooper et al., 2024 ) ; we carry both over to the recurrent state unchanged. Of the three scaling policies we compare, dynamic takes the per-step absmax, s t , c = max ⁡ | S t , c | / q max s_{t,c}=\max|S_{t,c}|/q_{\max} . Static (persistent) uses one offline-calibrated fixed scale, collected over multiple held-out sequences and timepoints and chosen to be constrained-MSE-optimal. Group-wise is persistent with a separate scale for each group of G = 32 G=32 state channels, at 5.0 5.0 bits per element against 4.0 4.0 for the per-channel policies.

sections.heading: Tasks and protocol.
sections.text: (a) NIAH recall with fictional needles, in the needle-in-a-haystack family ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) (paired McNemar). (b) Natural long-document continuation : process H H real tokens with per-step quantization, then teacher-force 256 natural tokens and measure per-document excess negative log-likelihood (NLL) against the unquantized model. A zero-state control confirms each task uses the recurrent state, and calibration and test are article-disjoint (independent WikiText-103 articles ( Merity et al., 2017 ) ). For the exposure analysis we fix total context to 2048 and vary only the quantized exposure H H : the last H H steps are quantized, the first 2048 − H 2048-H are an unquantized warm-up, so every H H predicts the same continuation.

sections.heading: Statistics.
sections.text: All comparisons are paired by document or by seed, and effects are reported with t t and discordant counts. The exposure × \times policy interaction is a difference-in-differences. Sample sizes differ by experiment and are given with each result: 12 or 16 seeds for the recall probes, 16 documents for the continuation and containment experiments, 18 held-out articles for the allocation audit, and 30 for the survival analysis.

sections.heading: 4 The failure frontier
sections.text: The usual way to report a state quantizer is to name a bit-width. Sweeping bit-width against decode horizon shows what that leaves out (Figure 1 a; exact recall values in Appendix Table 5 ). On GDN, INT8 is safe at every horizon measured, INT5 degrades gradually, INT4 collapses, and INT3 fails immediately, and the pattern is orthogonal to model scale, replicating at 0.8B and 2B. Mamba-2-1.3B has the same frontier at a longer length scale: INT4 recall is intact at H = 1024 H=1024 , where GDN-0.8B is already at 0.08 0.08 , and falls to 0.33 0.33 by H = 2048 H=2048 ; INT8 holds through H = 2048 H=2048 and falls to 0.08 0.08 at H = 4096 H=4096 , where the unquantized model still answers 0.75 0.75 . At H = 8192 H=8192 nothing answers, full precision included, which brackets the SSM frontier without tracing it. That is safety as the recall probe sees it. On natural continuation the same INT8 state costs 0.26 0.26 nats at H = 2048 H=2048 and 0.62 0.62 at H = 32768 H=32768 , a growth of 0.35 0.35 paired across contexts ( t = 10.9 t=10.9 ), and its perplexity penalty rises from 1.30 × 1.30\times the unquantized model to 1.85 × 1.85\times (Appendix E ). The bit-width that survives a needle test is still losing language-modelling quality as decode proceeds. Every configuration is also horizon-dependent. Recall at H = 0 H=0 is always intact, because the state has not yet been overwritten under quantization, and it decays as more decode steps pass through the quantizer. Lower bit-width is worse, longer horizon is worse, and the two axes are not separable. A bit-width therefore has to be reported together with the horizon at which it was measured, and this much holds independently of any mechanistic claim.

sections.heading: 5 Mechanism: a scale–state feedback loop
sections.text: The frontier says when INT4 breaks down, not why. The natural suspect is the part of the pipeline that looks most defensible. Per-token dynamic quantization re-derives the per-channel step size from the current state at every step, s t , c = max ⁡ | S t , c | / q max s_{t,c}=\max|S_{t,c}|/q_{\max} , which is exactly what one would do to track a moving distribution and is how KIVI scales the value cache ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Inside a recurrence it also couples the quantizer to its own output, and that coupling turns out to be destabilizing. Figure 2: The feedback, and cutting it. (a) Single-layer decode trajectory, boxcar smoothed. Norm and tail concentration get separate axes because they carry different units; both expand under dynamic INT4 and stay bounded under a persistent scale. (b) Taking the quantizer step size from the FP state instead of the quantized one removes the explosion at both scales. The three columns are independent arms, not a time course.

sections.heading: Numerical runaway is real and policy-driven.
sections.text: Under per-token dynamic INT4, the closed-loop recurrent-state norm grows super-linearly with decode length (Figure 1 b). On independent articles at H = 2048 H=2048 , the GDN state norm inflates from its unquantized value of ∼ 17 \sim 17 to 3.9 × 10 3 3.9\times 10^{3} at 0.8B and 2.2 × 10 4 2.2\times 10^{4} at 2B. A persistent fixed-range static quantizer holds the same norm at ∼ 17 \sim 17 – 18 18 , and a low clip rate is enough to do it: static scaling that clips 0.02% of elements already prevents the explosion. Mamba-2-1.3B differs in degree: the same policy grows the SSM-state norm only from 21.8 21.8 to 39 39 – 42 42 across runs, a factor of 1.8 1.8 – 1.9 1.9 , yet function still collapses at long horizon (§ 7 ). The numerical severity is architecture-dependent; the functional failure is not.

sections.heading: What the loop looks like step by step.
sections.text: Within a dynamic decode, three quantities co-expand: the per-channel scale, the tail concentration p 99.9 / p 50 p_{99.9}/p_{50} of | S | |S| , and the state norm. In a representative layer the tail ratio runs from 1.2 × 10 3 1.2\times 10^{3} to 6.1 × 10 3 6.1\times 10^{3} and the norm from 2.8 2.8 to 98 98 (Figure 2 a), whereas static quantization keeps all three bounded. That is what an outlier enlarging the scale, coarsening the bulk resolution, and admitting further error would look like, but the trajectory evidence is only correlational. The scale-vs-max relation is partly definitional, a bulk-resolution proxy did not monotonically collapse, and p 99.9 / p 50 p_{99.9}/p_{50} is unstable on near-sparse states. The loop is the cause of the runaway, and is consistent with, but not proven to be, the whole path to functional loss.

sections.heading: Causal identification via scale-yoking.
sections.text: We cut the feedback edge directly. Running the FP and a per-token-dynamic-INT4 model in lockstep on the same tokens, we yoke the quantizer step at each layer to the FP state, s t = max ⁡ | S t FP | / q max s_{t}=\max|S_{t}^{\mathrm{FP}}|/q_{\max} . The state is still quantized at every step, but the scale no longer depends on the runaway quantized state. Yoking eliminates the numerical explosion (Figure 2 b). At H = 2048 H=2048 the mean GDN-0.8B state norm falls from a self-scaled 3.5 × 10 4 3.5\times 10^{4} to 21 21 under yoking, against an unquantized 17 17 . That mean is driven by 5 of 16 articles above 10 3 10^{3} ; the median tells the same story less dramatically, 268 268 self-scaled against 21 21 and 17 17 . The 2B result has the same shape, 1.1 × 10 4 1.1\times 10^{4} falling to 20 20 . The self-scaled mean is heavy-tailed and spans two orders of magnitude across runs, while excess NLL for the same condition varies by under 2 % 2\% , so only its order of magnitude should be read as a finding (Appendix C ). The functional recovery is far smaller than the numerical one. Yoking returns 1.82 1.82 nats of excess NLL at 0.8B, from 5.39 5.39 to 3.57 3.57 (paired t = − 13.1 t=-13.1 ), and 1.35 1.35 nats at 2B ( t = − 6.9 t=-6.9 ). Two thirds of the damage survives an intervention that removes the runaway completely. The two failures are separable, and whatever accounts for the residual is not a stability problem (§ 8 ).

sections.heading: 6 What contains the loop
sections.text: The numerical half, at least, is containable, and which remedies work says what the loop is made of.

sections.heading: A ceiling on the scale, not a hunt for outliers.
sections.text: Outliers drive the scale in weight and activation quantization, and the methods that work there isolate or rescale them ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) . Two candidate remedies can be separated with matched-rate controls (Table 1 ). The first caps the dynamic scale at a ceiling c c taken from held-out calibration, s = min ⁡ ( max ⁡ | S | / q max , c ) s=\min(\max|S|/q_{\max},\,c) . Adding exact preservation of the overflowing elements on top of that cap changes nothing, moving excess NLL by 0.18 0.18 nats ( t = 1.53 t=1.53 ): keeping the outliers exactly does not help, so it is the scale ceiling that matters. The second remedy interrupts the loop in time. Zeroing the recurrent state every K K steps recovers about two nats of the dynamic runaway at H = 2048 H=2048 (Table 1 ), and the benefit is insensitive to K ∈ { 128,256,512 } K\in\{128,256,512\} . A persistent calibrated scale goes further and removes the edge: a scale that never reads the state cannot be driven by it. Capping, periodic reset, and persistent calibration bound, interrupt, and eliminate the same edge, which is why the methods of § 8 that instead locate outliers fail.

sections.heading: Numerical containment ≠ \neq functional preservation.
sections.text: Bounding the norm does not by itself preserve function. Static-INT5 keeps the norm near 17 17 across horizons and still incurs excess NLL ranging from 1.75 1.75 to 5.1 5.1 across conditions. Bounded norm does not imply bounded functional loss, and a static policy is not a constant NLL bias.

sections.heading: Removing the feedback is necessary; one scale is not always enough.
sections.text: Among the policies that remove the edge, how many scales they spend separates the architectures (Table 2 ). On both GDN models a single persistent scale is worse than discarding the recurrent state outright, by 1.77 1.77 nats at 0.8B ( t = 15.2 t=15.2 , no article better) and indistinguishably at 2B ( t = 0.04 t=0.04 ), while persistent group-wise INT4, which spends four scales where static spends one, beats the control by 0.99 0.99 and 1.93 1.93 nats. On Mamba-2 the ordering reverses: one scale already beats discarding the state ( t = − 5.00 t=-5.00 , 16 of 16 articles), and the extra scales cost 0.16 0.16 nats ( t = 2.39 t=2.39 ) while raising the modeled rate from 4.0 4.0 to 5.0 5.0 bits per element (§ 3 ). Per-token dynamic INT4 is worse than discarding the state in all three models. The feedback behaves the same way in both architectures. How many scales it then takes to leave a state worth keeping does not transfer. sections.heading: 7 Policy × \times exposure
sections.text: If the damage accumulates through the recurrence, then which policy is best cannot be a fixed answer: it has to depend on how long the state has been quantized. Using the matched-target continuation protocol of § 3 on independent articles, Figure 3 reports the excess NLL of per-token dynamic, persistent static, and group-wise INT4 across models. Figure 3: Policy × \times exposure. Excess NLL against quantized exposure H H , 16 independent documents per point, total context fixed at 2048 so every H H predicts the same continuation. The dynamic − - static gap widens with H H in all three models; whether dynamic is outright better at short H H is model-dependent. Dotted line: zero-state control floor.

sections.heading: The adaptive policy is the one that decays.
sections.text: The policy that tracks the distribution most faithfully is also the one whose disadvantage grows with every step of exposure: for every model, the dynamic − - static excess-NLL gap widens monotonically. We measure the interaction as a difference-in-differences, the growth in that gap between H = 512 H=512 and H = 2048 H=2048 , and it is positive and significant in all three models. GDN-0.8B widens by 1.22 1.22 nats ( t = 6.9 t=6.9 ) and GDN-2B by 1.80 1.80 ( t = 7.3 t=7.3 ); Mamba-1.3B widens by 5.06 5.06 ( t = 12.9 t=12.9 ), and an independent two-point run on that model replicates the effect at 4.83 4.83 ( t = 14.0 t=14.0 ). Persistent calibration therefore becomes more valuable, and per-token dynamic scaling more dangerous, precisely in the long-context regime these architectures are built for.

sections.heading: And at short exposure it often looks like the better choice.
sections.text: In two of our three models dynamic is outright ahead at H = 512 H=512 , for GDN-0.8B ( t = − 5.32 t=-5.32 ) and Mamba-1.3B ( t = − 13.81 t=-13.81 ), so a benchmark run at that length would select it. The five-point curve of Figure 3 puts the GDN-0.8B crossover between H = 1024 H=1024 , where dynamic is still marginally ahead, and H = 1536 H=1536 , where static has taken the lead. GDN-2B never shows the reversal. Static wins there at every exposure, including H = 512 H=512 ( t = + 2.64 t=+2.64 ), so the gap only widens monotonically. Mamba-2 reverses abruptly instead, from + 0.46 +0.46 nats at H = 1536 H=1536 to − 4.81 -4.81 at H = 2048 H=2048 . The claim we are entitled to is therefore the narrower one. Per-token dynamic scaling degrades relative to persistent calibration monotonically with quantized exposure across architectures and scales, and whether it also loses outright at short exposure depends on the model.

sections.heading: Decomposition.
sections.text: A history-only variant, which stops quantizing during the scored continuation, shows no crossover at all. Dynamic’s corrupted history is worse at every exposure, by 0.45 0.45 , 1.66 1.66 , and 2.95 2.95 nats at H = 512 H=512 , 1024 1024 , and 2048 2048 . Dynamic’s short-exposure advantage in the full pipeline therefore comes from its lower cost during the continuation stage, not from better history retention, and the crossover is the point at which its accumulating history damage overtakes that lower per-step cost. Static pays a higher but roughly stable per-step cost and accumulates little, its history damage growing only from 0.39 0.39 to 0.99 0.99 over the same range. Dynamic pays little per step and accumulates steeply, from 0.84 0.84 to 3.94 3.94 . That split is what containment predicts. We do not treat the full and history-only losses as strictly additive, because the two branches follow different state trajectories during the scored continuation.

sections.heading: 8 Where the residual does not come from
sections.text: Containment explains the exposure ranking of § 7 , but not the residual that yoking left behind. Either the grid is too coarse, or rounding error accumulates over thousands of steps, since the state is re-quantized at every step whether or not the scale is yoked. The two differ in what bit-width should do, so we repeat the yoking experiment from INT3 to INT8 (Table 3 ). Scale yoked, H = 2048 H=2048 INT3 INT4 INT5 INT6 INT8 excess NLL 4.82 3.57 2.96 1.56 0.31 Table 3: The residual thins with bit-width, which an accumulation floor would not do. GDN-0.8B, 16 held-out articles, scale yoked throughout so the feedback cannot confound the sweep. The INT4 arms reproduce the 5.39 5.39 self-scaled and 3.57 3.57 yoked of § 5 to four decimal places. The residual falls monotonically in 15 of the 16 articles, and 8.7 % 8.7\% of it survives at INT8, where the paired gap to INT4 is 3.26 3.26 nats ( t = 32.5 t=32.5 ). Accumulated rounding error would not fall away like this. The residual is a resolution limit : more bits buy it back, and a cleverer arrangement of the same bits does not.

sections.heading: Stochastic rounding is not the remedy.
sections.text: Round-to-nearest is biased, and bias is what compounds through a recurrence, so stochastic rounding ( Gupta et al., 2015 ) is the standard fix and the one the Nemotron 3 line ships for its SSM cache ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) . It costs 6.71 6.71 nats on top of yoked INT4 ( t = 41.1 t=41.1 ) and 5.77 5.77 on top of self-scaled INT4 ( t = 17.2 t=17.2 ), falling to 0.62 0.62 at INT8 ( t = 10.5 t=10.5 ). Removing the bias makes each step’s error larger— 2 \sqrt{2} in RMS, 1.42 × 1.42\times measured on the states—and a recurrence amplifies magnitude, not sign. Against exposure it holds all three policies between 9.7 9.7 and 11.2 11.2 nats out to 32K, worse at every checkpoint than clearing the state (Appendix D ).

sections.heading: Three ways of spending the same bits.
sections.text: Each of the following gives the quantizer more information than uniform group-wise scaling does, after the outlier-aware designs that work on weights, activations and the KV cache ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Hooper et al., 2024 ) , and each is beaten by it. • Outlier-frequency channel targeting / exact sparse escape. Giving extra bits to the most frequently-overflowing channels, or storing overflowing elements exactly, does not beat a random channel subset or uniform allocation—locating outliers is not containing the feedback. • Dynamic → \to static and static → \to dynamic hybrids. A hybrid that runs dynamic early and static late does beat both pure policies, because the late static caps the runaway. It still loses to group-wise ( t = − 14.2 t=-14.2 ). • Capped dynamic scaling. Beats static, loses to group-wise ( t = − 10.0 t=-10.0 ). Its exact-escape variant adds nothing (Table 1 ): the cap is what helps, not the escape. A temporal grid-churn account does not survive matched controls either.

sections.heading: Uniform group-wise scaling beats all three.
sections.text: Persistent group-wise INT4 is the least-damaging policy at every GDN model and horizon, at a lower modeled bit rate than uniform INT5. It beats persistent static INT4 by t = − 25 t=-25 to − 29 -29 at 0.8B and t = − 12 t=-12 at 2B, and it beats each design above by t = − 10 t=-10 to − 19 -19 (Table 1 ). Static and group-wise both remove the feedback edge and differ only in how many scales they spend on the channel axis, whereas every design above spends its extra information on finding outliers instead. This is the least damaging uniform policy on these models, and we did not invent any part of it.

sections.heading: A caution for practitioners.
sections.text: Even the best policy is far from lossless. At H = 2048 H=2048 uniform group-wise INT4 leaves natural-text perplexity at 7.8 × 7.8\times the unquantized model on 0.8B and 8.6 × 8.6\times on 2B, and the best leak-free allocation still costs 4.9 × 4.9\times and 7.4 × 7.4\times . Both pure INT4 policies are worse here than clearing the state altogether, so none of these options is usable. Quantization that preserves perfect NIAH recall can still severely damage general language-modeling quality : recall of a single planted fact is a far weaker probe of state fidelity than natural continuation. Figure 4: Per-layer allocation. (a) Quantizing one layer at a time, plotted at the true layer index; gaps are attention rather than linear-attention layers. (b) Rate–distortion. The connected series are an in-sample sweep, optimistic in level because the protected layers were chosen on the articles they are scored on. The star re-measures the same 4.0-bit policy under the leak-free protocol of Table 4 , and that gap is why the curves sit below the table.

sections.heading: Does per-layer mixed precision help? A leak-free test.
sections.text: Per-layer mixed precision is the natural refinement, because single-layer sensitivity is strongly concentrated. Quantizing one layer at a time to INT4, the first GDN layer alone accounts for 63 63 – 78 % 78\% of the summed single-layer damage at H = 2048 H=2048 (Figure 4 a). The obvious move is to protect a few layers at high precision and quantize the rest aggressively. We test that under a leak-free protocol, with calibration, selection, and test articles disjoint by title hash (6, 15, and 18 articles). Layer selection runs under the deployment quantizer, persistent group-wise, by marginal rescue from an all-INT2 baseline, and every reported number is on the held-out test articles (Table 4 , Figure 4 b). The positive finding. Extreme allocation—top-3 layers at INT8, the rest at INT2, averaging 4.0 bits—is a genuine Pareto improvement over uniform group-wise at a matched budget, beating uniform INT3 at the same 4.0 bits by t = − 12.8 t=-12.8 at 0.8B. It also beats uniform INT4 at a 20% lower rate, though that higher-rate margin attenuates with model scale, from t = − 10.3 t=-10.3 at 0.8B to t = − 2.2 t=-2.2 at 2B. Choosing the right layers is what does the work: the rescue-selected allocation beats random, inverse, and reconstruction-MSE-ranked allocations by t = − 17 t=-17 to − 22 -22 . The deflationary one. The sensitive layers are simply the first layers. Rescue selection, a matched-budget knapsack optimizer, and a trivial “protect the first three layers” baseline return numerically identical results, not merely similar ones (Table 4 ). No learned or search-based allocation adds anything over the trivial heuristic. Early recurrent layers dominate quantization sensitivity and protecting them helps at a fixed budget, but no sophisticated allocation is warranted, and even the first-layer advantage over spending the bits uniformly shrinks as models grow. sections.heading: 9 How long is a quantized state safe?
sections.text: Excess NLL averages over a window and hides when a policy first breaks, so we add a reliability view. Feeding the FP and a quantized model the same tokens, we record the first step at which the quantized model flips a next-token argmax that FP had predicted with a top-2 logit margin above 8. That first-passage failure time τ \tau is measured on 30 held-out articles up to H = 8 H=8 K, right-censored at article length. The survival curve Pr ⁡ ( τ > h ) \Pr(\tau>h) (Figure 5 ) orders the policies monotonically at every horizon, and at every FP-confidence threshold (Appendix F ): first-layer-protected group-wise, then group-wise, then static and dynamic together. At H = 2048 H=2048 , protected group-wise leaves 19 of 30 articles confident-token-faithful, group-wise 5 of 30, and the two pure policies none. There is no strategy reversal here. The best policy short is the best policy long, so on this metric short evaluation does not select the wrong policy, unlike the crossover of § 7 . But short evaluation badly underestimates risk. The deployment-preferred policy looks essentially lossless at short horizon, failing on 1 of 30 articles by H = 512 H=512 . By H = 2048 H=2048 it has failed on 11 of 30, and those long-horizon failures have no short-horizon precursor. It replicates at 2B: 0 of 30 by H = 512 H=512 , 12 of 30 by H = 2048 H=2048 . Failure horizons cannot be extrapolated from short traces either: a constant- or power-law-hazard fit to the first 256 steps mis-predicts survival at H = 2048 H=2048 by well over an octave, because the good policy has no short-window events to fit. Evaluating recurrent-state quantization at short length is hazardous not because it ranks policies wrongly, but because it certifies a policy as safe long before its failures appear.

sections.heading: What generalizes.
sections.text: A single-architecture result would not be worth much, so it matters that the exposure interaction (§ 7 ) and the failure frontier both replicate across GDN (0.8B, 2B) and Mamba-2 (1.3B), the frontier sitting about twice as far out on the SSM. Group-wise dominance does not: it holds at both GDN scales and fails on Mamba-2 (Table 2 ). Concurrent work approaches low-precision recurrent inference by other routes—decay-aware mixed precision applied to the state itself ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and a per-element floating-point format applied to weights and activations with the state left in high precision ( Kozyrev and Maiboroda, 2026 ) —neither of which we compare against here. Severity varies with architecture while the functional interaction does not, so the interaction belongs to quantized recurrent-state decoding and not to the delta rule.

sections.heading: One principle, four findings.
sections.text: The positive results are one idea seen four ways: a persistent scale eliminates the feedback edge, a calibrated ceiling bounds it, periodic reset interrupts it, and a higher bit-width merely delays the loop. That every outlier-locating policy failed is the same principle read backwards.

sections.heading: What we would tell a practitioner.
sections.text: Prefer any persistently calibrated scale over per-token dynamic scaling, check group-wise against plain static on the target architecture rather than assuming group-wise wins, protect the first recurrent layer, and expect little from learned allocation beyond that. The point we would most want carried forward is the reporting one: a bit-width certified at 512 steps says little about 4K and nothing about 32K, and the horizon is where low-bit recurrent-state inference actually breaks.

sections.heading: Limitations
sections.text: Measurement. We simulate quantization rather than implement a packed kernel, so bit rates are modeled and we report no latency or throughput. The best policy still leaves perplexity at 7.8 × 7.8\times (0.8B) and 8.6 × 8.6\times (2B) the unquantized model at H = 2048 H=2048 . We run no head-to-head against architecture-specific quantizers (Q-Mamba, Quamba2, DAMP), which differ in both what they quantize and at what rate, and make no systems claim. Scope and mechanism. Two architectures and three model sizes, all below 3B; the first-layer-protection advantage already shrinks from 0.8B to 2B, so we cannot say whether it survives at deployment scale. Scale-yoking identifies the feedback as the cause of the numerical runaway but recovers only part of the functional loss, and we do not identify the remainder; § 5 records the countervailing evidence and the run-to-run instability of the norm itself.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: This work is an empirical analysis of numerical stability in quantized inference. It uses publicly released model checkpoints and the public WikiText-103 corpus, introduces no new data collection, and involves no human subjects or personally identifying information. The synthetic recall probes are generated from fictional entities. The practical effect of the findings, if any, is to make low-bit long-context inference more reliable and to warn against a specific evaluation practice (certifying a quantizer at short decode length) that can overstate deployed reliability. We see no direct dual-use concern beyond those already attached to efficient LLM inference generally.

sections.heading: Reproducibility
sections.text: All experiments use public model checkpoints and the WikiText-103 corpus, and every run reported here fits on a single RTX 3090. Code, result files and the project page are at https://avalon-s.github.io/dynamic-scaling-fails/ . The release carries the fake-quantization, calibration and evaluation code, the article-disjoint calibration/selection/test splits by title hash, the result file behind every number reported here, the plotting scripts that build every figure directly from those files, and the per-run provenance (article IDs, quantizer, group size, model and data revision). GDN runs are bit-identical between independent executions: re-running the long-horizon sweep of Appendix E from scratch reproduced all 35 per-document excess-NLL values to the last digit. The Mamba-2 runtime is not deterministic, and repeating the same configuration moves a single-document loss by a few hundredths of a nat, so Mamba numbers should be read as reproducible in distribution rather than exactly. State norms reproduce far less well than losses, because a runaway amplifies whatever differs between runs: across three executions the dynamic-INT4 norm at H = 2048 H=2048 ranges from 38.9 38.9 to 42.3 42.3 while the corresponding excess NLL moves by 0.4 % 0.4\% . Read a norm from a runaway condition to one significant figure.

sections.heading: Appendix C Additional protocol notes
sections.text: Zero-state control. For every task, clearing the recurrent state each step (rather than quantizing it) collapses performance to the no-context floor (excess NLL 2.3 2.3 – 4.1 4.1 across models and horizons; the dotted line in Figure 3 ), confirming the tasks genuinely exercise the recurrent state. Boundary reset. The periodic-reset result (Table 1 ) zeros the state on a fixed schedule. Its benefit is insensitive to the period: excess NLL is 3.38 3.38 , 3.68 3.68 , and 3.44 3.44 for K ∈ { 128,256,512 } K\in\{128,256,512\} . A tuned corruption schedule would depend on the period; interrupting the accumulation does not. What the state is worth in memory. The recurrent state is fixed in size. An attention KV cache is not, so the share of decode memory the state accounts for falls as context grows. Qwen3.5-0.8B carries 18 linear layers of 16 × 128 × 128 16\times 128\times 128 FP32 state, 18 18 MB in all, against six attention layers with two KV heads of dimension 256 in BF16, 12 12 KB per token. That is 43 % 43\% of the cache at 2K, 16 % 16\% at 8K, 4.5 % 4.5\% at 32K and 1.2 % 1.2\% at 128K. Mamba-2-1.3B has no attention layers at all, so its 96 96 MB of state is the whole cache at every length. The case for quantizing the state is strongest in pure SSMs and at moderate context. What this paper measures is the cost of doing it. State-norm provenance. The two self-scaled means quoted in § 5 come from different runs on disjoint articles, 3.9 × 10 3 3.9\times 10^{3} from the exposure sweep and 3.5 × 10 4 3.5\times 10^{4} from the yoking run. The distribution is heavy-tailed. On the yoking run 5 of 16 articles exceed 10 3 10^{3} , and the median is 268 268 against that mean. Excess NLL for the same condition moves by under 2 % 2\% across the same runs, so the functional measurements are stable where the norm is not. Multi-key retrieval and per-model exposure curves are reported with the released code.

sections.heading: Appendix D What the residual is made of
sections.text: § 8 reads the residual that survives yoking as a resolution limit, on the evidence of a bit-width sweep and against the alternative that rounding error accumulates. This section carries the exposure half of that comparison, which does not fit there, and the protocol both probes share. All of it runs on the 16 held-out articles of § 5 .

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: Both probes hold the scale yoked. The bit-width sweep and the stochastic-rounding penalties are in § 8 ; stochastic rounding replaces the deterministic round with ⌊ x / s + u ⌋ \lfloor x/s+u\rfloor , u ∼ U ⁡ ( 0 , 1 ) u\sim U(0,1) . Against exposure, on the seven long contexts of Appendix E , the effect is larger. The unquantized reference is bit-identical across the two jobs at every checkpoint, so the policies pair by document. Stochastic rounding holds all three policies between 9.7 9.7 and 11.2 11.2 nats at every horizon from 2K to 32K, where round-to-nearest separates them by 2.0 2.0 to 5.9 5.9 . The distinctions the rest of the paper draws mostly vanish. Persistent static and group-wise differ by 2.76 2.76 nats under round-to-nearest at H = 32768 H=32768 ( t = 9.3 t=9.3 ) and by 0.54 0.54 under stochastic rounding ( t = 1.6 t=1.6 ). It also leaves the model worse off than clearing the state entirely, exceeding the zero-state control by 6.6 6.6 to 7.1 7.1 nats at every checkpoint ( t = 19 t=19 to 32 32 ).

sections.heading: Appendix E The curve past 2048
sections.text: Fixing total context at 2048 is what lets every H H predict the same continuation, and it is also a ceiling. It cannot be lifted by running longer: the held-out corpus contains no article longer than 16,227 16{,}227 tokens, so a 32K single-article context does not exist to be measured. This appendix uses a second protocol. Each context is quantized from the first decode step, and a 256-token continuation is scored at H ∈ { 2048 , 4096 , 8192 , 16384 , 32768 } H\in\{2048,4096,8192,16384,32768\} . Excess NLL is still the quantized minus unquantized loss on the same tokens at the same position, so the drift of natural perplexity with position cancels in the difference rather than entering it. Seven contexts of 33,024 33{,}024 tokens are built by concatenating held-out articles; no article appears in two contexts, nor in the six articles used for calibration. The two protocols coincide at H = 2048 H=2048 , and that overlap is the check. sections.heading: How long the state stays worth keeping.
sections.text: Excess NLL says how much a policy costs, not whether the state it maintains is still worth maintaining. Running the same seven contexts with the recurrent state zeroed at every step answers that directly. Group-wise INT4 beats the zeroed state by 1.23 1.23 nats at H = 2048 H=2048 ( t = − 7.4 t=-7.4 ), and the margin decays with exposure: 0.63 0.63 at H = 4096 H=4096 , 0.45 0.45 at H = 8192 H=8192 , 0.24 0.24 at H = 16384 H=16384 , and 0.00 0.00 at H = 32768 H=32768 ( t = 0.0 t=0.0 ). Past roughly 16K the difference stops being detectable at this sample size, and at 32K the quantized state carries no more of the context forward than discarding it would. The zeroed control itself is flat across horizon, at 2.98 2.98 to 3.30 3.30 nats, inside the 2.3 2.3 – 4.1 4.1 band this control gives elsewhere in the paper. This also settles how to read a curve that flattens. Per-token dynamic sits three times the floor at H = 32768 H=32768 and has been above it since H = 2048 H=2048 , so its deceleration after 8K is exhaustion rather than containment. Group-wise flattens nowhere in the range, and converges on the floor from below instead.

sections.heading: What “safe” means for INT8.
sections.text: The frontier of § 4 calls INT8 safe at every horizon it measures, on the evidence of a recall probe that returns 1.00 1.00 throughout. Natural continuation disagrees. Under the same protocol, group-wise INT8 costs 0.26 0.26 nats at H = 2048 H=2048 and 0.62 0.62 at H = 32768 H=32768 , growing by 0.35 0.35 paired across contexts ( t = 10.9 t=10.9 ); its perplexity penalty is 1.30 × 1.30\times the unquantized model at the short horizon and 1.85 × 1.85\times at the long one. Group-wise INT5 sits between, at 1.84 1.84 and 3.11 3.11 nats.

sections.heading: Scale and architecture.
sections.text: The growth replicates at 2B and more strongly: group-wise INT4 adds 1.70 1.70 nats between H = 2048 H=2048 and H = 32768 H=32768 ( t = 8.0 t=8.0 ), static 1.42 1.42 ( t = 4.5 t=4.5 ). Per-token dynamic diverges out of bfloat16 range on one of the seven contexts before H = 16384 H=16384 , so its 2B growth of 3.06 3.06 nats ( t = 5.5 t=5.5 ) is over the six that remain finite; the numerical runaway of § 5 becomes an actual overflow at this scale. Mamba-2-1.3B does not replicate it. Over the same seven contexts the SSM state shows no significant growth past H = 2048 H=2048 under either policy, − 0.26 -0.26 nats for dynamic ( t = − 0.5 t=-0.5 ) and + 0.68 +0.68 for static ( t = 1.9 t=1.9 ), though dynamic is already 7.06 7.06 nats behind at H = 2048 H=2048 and static remains ahead of it by t = 9.2 t=9.2 at H = 32768 H=32768 . Whether the long-horizon accumulation is specific to the delta-rule family or harder to resolve against this runtime’s nondeterminism is not settled by seven documents.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.15139v1 [cs.LG] 10 Oct 2026 When Dynamic Scaling Fails: A Scale–State Feedback Governs Recurrent-State Quantization in Linear-Attention and SSM LLMs Yuhang Jiang Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: jyhtjtj@gmail.com Abstract Linear-attention and state-space LLMs carry long context in a fixed-size recurrent state, and quantizing that state is the natural way to cut its cost during long decode. Unlike a weight tensor, the state is rewritten at every step, so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound. INT4 that leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at the start destroys it a thousand steps later. The mechanism is a feedback between the quantizer scale and the state it is derived from. Yoking that scale to a full-precision reference removes the resulting norm explosion entirely, yet recovers only 1.8 of the 5.4 nats lost, so numerical instability and functional degradation are separable failures. The remainder is a resolution problem that locating outliers does not solve, since every outlier-aware scheme here loses to plain persistent scaling. Allocating bits across layers does help, but under article-disjoint splits a learned allocation collapses onto the trivial rule of protecting the first few layers. Run out to 32K, group-wise INT4 is worth no more than discarding the state. Contain the scale rather than locate outliers, and report the decode horizon at which a bit-width was certified. 1 Introduction Suppose you quantize the recurrent state of a linear-attention model to INT4 and check it the usual way, with needle-in-a-haystack retrieval. Recall comes back perfect at every length you measure, so you ship it. Past the longest length you tested, the best of the four-bit policies still recovers the planted needle on demand, and its perplexity on ordinary text has risen eightfold. It remembers the fact and has stopped being a language model. Both halves of that story are measured below, and both are invisible to the way recurrent-state quantization is currently reported. Linear-attention and state-space models replace the growing KV cache of softmax attention with a fixed-size recurrent state : Gated DeltaNet (GDN) powers the linear layers of Qwen3-Next ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) , Kimi Linear ( Kimi Team, 2025 ) builds on it, and Mamba-2 is a widely used SSM. That state is a real deployment cost during long decode, so quantizing it is the natural remedy. But a recurrent state is not a weight tensor. It is rewritten at every decode step , so a quantizer applied at each step sits inside the recurrence and its errors compound, and a bit-width certified as safe at short exposure need not stay safe as decode proceeds . Per-token dynamic INT4 leaves synthetic recall perfectly intact at H = 0 H=0 and destroys it by H = 1024 H=1024 (Figure 1 a). Three things have kept that axis out of view. The closest developed literature is low-bit KV-cache quantization ( Hooper et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) , where the cache is stored rather than recurrent, so error never re-enters the state and exposure is not reported as a variable. Quantization research more broadly grew up on weights and activations ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ; Frantar et al., 2023 ) , neither of which carries its own quantization error into the next step. And the probe everyone reaches for is retrieval accuracy, which turns out to be the least sensitive instrument available for this failure. The eightfold rise in the opening paragraph is what that insensitivity costs, and a warning in its own right. Figure 1: The phenomenon. (a) NIAH recall over 12 seeds against quantized decode horizon H H . Every bit-width is intact at H = 0 H=0 and decays as the state is overwritten; INT5 traces the frontier. (b) Mean recurrent-state norm on independent articles, log scale: per-token dynamic INT4 inflates it by two to three orders of magnitude, while the static curves and the unquantized reference coincide along the bottom. Nothing is measured between H = 0 H=0 and H = 1024 H=1024 , so that span is dotted; 2B was not run at H = 8192 H=8192 . Prior work quantizes these caches with architecture-specific machinery: Q-Mamba ( Chen et al., 2025 ) reaches an INT4 Mamba-2 state cache via trained DSQ/ESR alongside weights and activations, and the Nemotron 3 line ships FP16 with stochastic rounding for the Mamba SSM cache ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) . We instead study state-only, training-free fake-quantization , to isolate what the recurrence does to quantization error independently of any trained corrector. We contribute: • A failure frontier in (bit-width × \times decode horizon), making decode horizon an explicit stability axis for recurrent-cache quantization (§ 4 ). • A scale–state feedback mechanism for per-token dynamic scaling, causally identified by a scale-yoking intervention that removes the numerical runaway but only part of the functional loss, and a unifying account of containment that explains why a calibrated ceiling, periodic reset and persistent scaling all work, and why which of them works best depends on the architecture (§ 5 , § 6 ). • A universal policy × \times exposure interaction with a model-dependent short-horizon reversal, replicated on independent articles across architectures and scales (§ 7 ). • A negative result : every outlier-locating allocation loses to plain group-wise scaling, while per-layer allocation helps only to collapse onto a trivial rule (§ 8 ), and a survival analysis showing that short evaluations certify policies as safe long before their failures appear (§ 9 ). 2 Related work Linear-attention and state-space LLMs. Linear attention replaces softmax attention with a kernel-feature recurrence and a fixed-size state ( Katharopoulos et al., 2020 ) ; the delta rule sharpens that recurrence ( Schlag et al., 2021 ; Yang et al., 2024 ) , and Gated DeltaNet ( Yang et al., 2025 ) is the linear component of Qwen3-Next ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) , while Kimi Linear ( Kimi Team, 2025 ) extends it with finer-grained gating. State-space models ( Gu and Dao, 2024 ; Dao and Gu, 2024 ) carry context in an SSM state. All of them share the property we study: a fixed-size recurrent state, overwritten each step. Cache quantization. For softmax attention the analogous target is the growing KV cache, and low-bit KV-cache quantization is well developed ( Hooper et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) . The recurrent case differs: the cache is constant-size but recurrent , so each step’s error enters the state that produces the next one. Beyond Q-Mamba ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , Quamba2 ( Chiang et al., 2025 ) quantizes Mamba weights and activations (W8A8 through W4A16) together with the inputs of the linear recurrence, MambaQuant ( Xu et al., 2025 ) applies variance-aligning rotations to weights and activations, and ReplaySSM ( Dao, 2026 ) recomputes state from cached inputs rather than quantizing it at all. Of these only Q-Mamba reaches the persistent state, and only alongside weights and activations. Concurrent work DAMP ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) quantizes the GDN and KDA state directly, choosing high-risk channels offline by quantization-error energy and decay persistence. It runs at about 9.9 bits per state value on 35B and 48B models, with deployment kernels, and reports that INT4 and NVFP4 collapse accuracy. We hold everything else in full precision, work below five bits, and vary how long the state is quantized, an axis DAMP holds fixed. Kozyrev and Maiboroda (2026) instead quantize weights and activations of a hybrid 27B model and find injected noise flat over 32K tokens. There the stored state stays in high precision, so the scale never becomes a function of the corrupted state. Outliers and group-wise quantization. A large body of LLM-quantization work targets activation outliers—mixed-precision on outlier channels ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , migrating outlier scale into weights ( Xiao et al., 2023 ) , second-order error compensation ( Frantar et al., 2023 ) , and activation-aware protection of salient weights ( Lin et al., 2024 ) —and group-wise scaling is a standard remedy. Locating the outlier channels does not beat uniform group-wise quantization, because the recurrent failure is a scale–state feedback to be contained rather than a static set of outliers to be handled. Sensitivity-aware mixed precision is likewise well established, from Hessian-trace layer allocation ( Dong et al., 2020 ) to layer-wise KV precision search ( Li et al., 2025 ) and per-head rate-distortion allocation ( Zuo et al., 2026 ) . Our leak-free audit (§ 8 ) shows this machinery is unnecessary here: sensitivity is so concentrated in the first layers that a learned allocator, a knapsack optimizer, and a trivial protect-first-few-layers baseline coincide. 3 Setup Models. Qwen3.5-0.8B and Qwen3.5-2B (official Gated DeltaNet hybrid ( Yang et al., 2025 ; Qwen Team, 2026 ) , 262K context, BF16 compute with FP32 recurrent state) and Mamba-2-1.3B ( Dao and Gu, 2024 ) ( state-spaces , native loader). The GDN recurrent state has shape ( 1 , 16 , 128 , 128 ) (1,16,128,128) ; the Mamba SSM state ( 1 , 64 , 64 , 128 ) (1,64,64,128) . Quantization. We apply symmetric per-channel INT- b b fake-quantization to the recurrent state at each decode step: round, clamp, dequantize. Scaling at channel or vector granularity is the standard response to activation outliers ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ) , and group-wise scaling the one KV-cache quantizers use ( Liu et al., 2024 ; Hooper et al., 2024 ) ; we carry both over to the recurrent state unchanged. Of the three scaling policies we compare, dynamic takes the per-step absmax, s t , c = max ⁡ | S t , c | / q max s_{t,c}=\max|S_{t,c}|/q_{\max} . Static (persistent) uses one offline-calibrated fixed scale, collected over multiple held-out sequences and timepoints and chosen to be constrained-MSE-optimal. Group-wise is persistent with a separate scale for each group of G = 32 G=32 state channels, at 5.0 5.0 bits per element against 4.0 4.0 for the per-channel policies. Tasks and protocol. (a) NIAH recall with fictional needles, in the needle-in-a-haystack family ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) (paired McNemar). (b) Natural long-document continuation : process H H real tokens with per-step quantization, then teacher-force 256 natural tokens and measure per-document excess negative log-likelihood (NLL) against the unquantized model. A zero-state control confirms each task uses the recurrent state, and calibration and test are article-disjoint (independent WikiText-103 articles ( Merity et al., 2017 ) ). For the exposure analysis we fix total context to 2048 and vary only the quantized exposure H H : the last H H steps are quantized, the first 2048 − H 2048-H are an unquantized warm-up, so every H H predicts the same continuation. Statistics. All comparisons are paired by document or by seed, and effects are reported with t t and discordant counts. The exposure × \times policy interaction is a difference-in-differences. Sample sizes differ by experiment and are given with each result: 12 or 16 seeds for the recall probes, 16 documents for the continuation and containment experiments, 18 held-out articles for the allocation audit, and 30 for the survival analysis. 4 The failure frontier The usual way to report a state quantizer is to name a bit-width. Sweeping bit-width against decode horizon shows what that leaves out (Figure 1 a; exact recall values in Appendix Table 5 ). On GDN, INT8 is safe at every horizon measured, INT5 degrades gradually, INT4 collapses, and INT3 fails immediately, and the pattern is orthogonal to model scale, replicating at 0.8B and 2B. Mamba-2-1.3B has the same frontier at a longer length scale: INT4 recall is intact at H = 1024 H=1024 , where GDN-0.8B is already at 0.08 0.08 , and falls to 0.33 0.33 by H = 2048 H=2048 ; INT8 holds through H = 2048 H=2048 and falls to 0.08 0.08 at H = 4096 H=4096 , where the unquantized model still answers 0.75 0.75 . At H = 8192 H=8192 nothing answers, full precision included, which brackets the SSM frontier without tracing it. That is safety as the recall probe sees it. On natural continuation the same INT8 state costs 0.26 0.26 nats at H = 2048 H=2048 and 0.62 0.62 at H = 32768 H=32768 , a growth of 0.35 0.35 paired across contexts ( t = 10.9 t=10.9 ), and its perplexity penalty rises from 1.30 × 1.30\times the unquantized model to 1.85 × 1.85\times (Appendix E ). The bit-width that survives a needle test is still losing language-modelling quality as decode proceeds. Every configuration is also horizon-dependent. Recall at H = 0 H=0 is always intact, because the state has not yet been overwritten under quantization, and it decays as more decode steps pass through the quantizer. Lower bit-width is worse, longer horizon is worse, and the two axes are not separable. A bit-width therefore has to be reported together with the horizon at which it was measured, and this much holds independently of any mechanistic claim. 5 Mechanism: a scale–state feedback loop The frontier says when INT4 breaks down, not why. The natural suspect is the part of the pipeline that looks most defensible. Per-token dynamic quantization re-derives the per-channel step size from the current state at every step, s t , c = max ⁡ | S t , c | / q max s_{t,c}=\max|S_{t,c}|/q_{\max} , which is exactly what one would do to track a moving distribution and is how KIVI scales the value cache ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Inside a recurrence it also couples the quantizer to its own output, and that coupling turns out to be destabilizing. Figure 2: The feedback, and cutting it. (a) Single-layer decode trajectory, boxcar smoothed. Norm and tail concentration get separate axes because they carry different units; both expand under dynamic INT4 and stay bounded under a persistent scale. (b) Taking the quantizer step size from the FP state instead of the quantized one removes the explosion at both scales. The three columns are independent arms, not a time course. Numerical runaway is real and policy-driven. Under per-token dynamic INT4, the closed-loop recurrent-state norm grows super-linearly with decode length (Figure 1 b). On independent articles at H = 2048 H=2048 , the GDN state norm inflates from its unquantized value of ∼ 17 \sim 17 to 3.9 × 10 3 3.9\times 10^{3} at 0.8B and 2.2 × 10 4 2.2\times 10^{4} at 2B. A persistent fixed-range static quantizer holds the same norm at ∼ 17 \sim 17 – 18 18 , and a low clip rate is enough to do it: static scaling that clips 0.02% of elements already prevents the explosion. Mamba-2-1.3B differs in degree: the same policy grows the SSM-state norm only from 21.8 21.8 to 39 39 – 42 42 across runs, a factor of 1.8 1.8 – 1.9 1.9 , yet function still collapses at long horizon (§ 7 ). The numerical severity is architecture-dependent; the functional failure is not. What the loop looks like step by step. Within a dynamic decode, three quantities co-expand: the per-channel scale, the tail concentration p 99.9 / p 50 p_{99.9}/p_{50} of | S | |S| , and the state norm. In a representative layer the tail ratio runs from 1.2 × 10 3 1.2\times 10^{3} to 6.1 × 10 3 6.1\times 10^{3} and the norm from 2.8 2.8 to 98 98 (Figure 2 a), whereas static quantization keeps all three bounded. That is what an outlier enlarging the scale, coarsening the bulk resolution, and admitting further error would look like, but the trajectory evidence is only correlational. The scale-vs-max relation is partly definitional, a bulk-resolution proxy did not monotonically collapse, and p 99.9 / p 50 p_{99.9}/p_{50} is unstable on near-sparse states. The loop is the cause of the runaway, and is consistent with, but not proven to be, the whole path to functional loss. Causal identification via scale-yoking. We cut the feedback edge directly. Running the FP and a per-token-dynamic-INT4 model in lockstep on the same tokens, we yoke the quantizer step at each layer to the FP state, s t = max ⁡ | S t FP | / q max s_{t}=\max|S_{t}^{\mathrm{FP}}|/q_{\max} . The state is still quantized at every step, but the scale no longer depends on the runaway quantized state. Yoking eliminates the numerical explosion (Figure 2 b). At H = 2048 H=2048 the mean GDN-0.8B state norm falls from a self-scaled 3.5 × 10 4 3.5\times 10^{4} to 21 21 under yoking, against an unquantized 17 17 . That mean is driven by 5 of 16 articles above 10 3 10^{3} ; the median tells the same story less dramatically, 268 268 self-scaled against 21 21 and 17 17 . The 2B result has the same shape, 1.1 × 10 4 1.1\times 10^{4} falling to 20 20 . The self-scaled mean is heavy-tailed and spans two orders of magnitude across runs, while excess NLL for the same condition varies by under 2 % 2\% , so only its order of magnitude should be read as a finding (Appendix C ). The functional recovery is far smaller than the numerical one. Yoking returns 1.82 1.82 nats of excess NLL at 0.8B, from 5.39 5.39 to 3.57 3.57 (paired t = − 13.1 t=-13.1 ), and 1.35 1.35 nats at 2B ( t = − 6.9 t=-6.9 ). Two thirds of the damage survives an intervention that removes the runaway completely. The two failures are separable, and whatever accounts for the residual is not a stability problem (§ 8 ). 6 What contains the loop The numerical half, at least, is containable, and which remedies work says what the loop is made of. A ceiling on the scale, not a hunt for outliers. Outliers drive the scale in weight and activation quantization, and the methods that work there isolate or rescale them ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ; Xiao et al., 2023 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) . Two candidate remedies can be separated with matched-rate controls (Table 1 ). The first caps the dynamic scale at a ceiling c c taken from held-out calibration, s = min ⁡ ( max ⁡ | S | / q max , c ) s=\min(\max|S|/q_{\max},\,c) . Adding exact preservation of the overflowing elements on top of that cap changes nothing, moving excess NLL by 0.18 0.18 nats ( t = 1.53 t=1.53 ): keeping the outliers exactly does not help, so it is the scale ceiling that matters. The second remedy interrupts the loop in time. Zeroing the recurrent state every K K steps recovers about two nats of the dynamic runaway at H = 2048 H=2048 (Table 1 ), and the benefit is insensitive to K ∈ { 128,256,512 } K\in\{128,256,512\} . A persistent calibrated scale goes further and removes the edge: a scale that never reads the state cannot be driven by it. Capping, periodic reset, and persistent calibration bound, interrupt, and eliminate the same edge, which is why the methods of § 8 that instead locate outliers fail. Numerical containment ≠ \neq functional preservation. Bounding the norm does not by itself preserve function. Static-INT5 keeps the norm near 17 17 across horizons and still incurs excess NLL ranging from 1.75 1.75 to 5.1 5.1 across conditions. Bounded norm does not imply bounded functional loss, and a static policy is not a constant NLL bias. Removing the feedback is necessary; one scale is not always enough. Among the policies that remove the edge, how many scales they spend separates the architectures (Table 2 ). On both GDN models a single persistent scale is worse than discarding the recurrent state outright, by 1.77 1.77 nats at 0.8B ( t = 15.2 t=15.2 , no article better) and indistinguishably at 2B ( t = 0.04 t=0.04 ), while persistent group-wise INT4, which spends four scales where static spends one, beats the control by 0.99 0.99 and 1.93 1.93 nats. On Mamba-2 the ordering reverses: one scale already beats discarding the state ( t = − 5.00 t=-5.00 , 16 of 16 articles), and the extra scales cost 0.16 0.16 nats ( t = 2.39 t=2.39 ) while raising the modeled rate from 4.0 4.0 to 5.0 5.0 bits per element (§ 3 ). Per-token dynamic INT4 is worse than discarding the state in all three models. The feedback behaves the same way in both architectures. How many scales it then takes to leave a state worth keeping does not transfer. Using the matched-target continuation protocol of § 3 on independent articles, Figure 3 reports the excess NLL of per-token dynamic, persistent static, and group-wise INT4 across models. Figure 3: Policy × \times exposure. Excess NLL against quantized exposure H H , 16 independent documents per point, total context fixed at 2048 so every H H predicts the same continuation. The dynamic − - static gap widens with H H in all three models; whether dynamic is outright better at short H H is model-dependent. Dotted line: zero-state control floor. The adaptive policy is the one that decays. The policy that tracks the distribution most faithfully is also the one whose disadvantage grows with every step of exposure: for every model, the dynamic − - static excess-NLL gap widens monotonically. We measure the interaction as a difference-in-differences, the growth in that gap between H = 512 H=512 and H = 2048 H=2048 , and it is positive and significant in all three models. GDN-0.8B widens by 1.22 1.22 nats ( t = 6.9 t=6.9 ) and GDN-2B by 1.80 1.80 ( t = 7.3 t=7.3 ); Mamba-1.3B widens by 5.06 5.06 ( t = 12.9 t=12.9 ), and an independent two-point run on that model replicates the effect at 4.83 4.83 ( t = 14.0 t=14.0 ). Persistent calibration therefore becomes more valuable, and per-token dynamic scaling more dangerous, precisely in the long-context regime these architectures are built for. And at short exposure it often looks like the better choice. In two of our three models dynamic is outright ahead at H = 512 H=512 , for GDN-0.8B ( t = − 5.32 t=-5.32 ) and Mamba-1.3B ( t = − 13.81 t=-13.81 ), so a benchmark run at that length would select it. The five-point curve of Figure 3 puts the GDN-0.8B crossover between H = 1024 H=1024 , where dynamic is still marginally ahead, and H = 1536 H=1536 , where static has taken the lead. GDN-2B never shows the reversal. Static wins there at every exposure, including H = 512 H=512 ( t = + 2.64 t=+2.64 ), so the gap only widens monotonically. Mamba-2 reverses abruptly instead, from + 0.46 +0.46 nats at H = 1536 H=1536 to − 4.81 -4.81 at H = 2048 H=2048 . The claim we are entitled to is therefore the narrower one. Per-token dynamic scaling degrades relative to persistent calibration monotonically with quantized exposure across architectures and scales, and whether it also loses outright at short exposure depends on the model. Decomposition. A history-only variant, which stops quantizing during the scored continuation, shows no crossover at all. Dynamic’s corrupted history is worse at every exposure, by 0.45 0.45 , 1.66 1.66 , and 2.95 2.95 nats at H = 512 H=512 , 1024 1024 , and 2048 2048 . Dynamic’s short-exposure advantage in the full pipeline therefore comes from its lower cost during the continuation stage, not from better history retention, and the crossover is the point at which its accumulating history damage overtakes that lower per-step cost. Static pays a higher but roughly stable per-step cost and accumulates little, its history damage growing only from 0.39 0.39 to 0.99 0.99 over the same range. Dynamic pays little per step and accumulates steeply, from 0.84 0.84 to 3.94 3.94 . That split is what containment predicts. We do not treat the full and history-only losses as strictly additive, because the two branches follow different state trajectories during the scored continuation. 8 Where the residual does not come from Containment explains the exposure ranking of § 7 , but not the residual that yoking left behind. Either the grid is too coarse, or rounding error accumulates over thousands of steps, since the state is re-quantized at every step whether or not the scale is yoked. The two differ in what bit-width should do, so we repeat the yoking experiment from INT3 to INT8 (Table 3 ). The residual falls monotonically in 15 of the 16 articles, and 8.7 % 8.7\% of it survives at INT8, where the paired gap to INT4 is 3.26 3.26 nats ( t = 32.5 t=32.5 ). Accumulated rounding error would not fall away like this. The residual is a resolution limit : more bits buy it back, and a cleverer arrangement of the same bits does not. Stochastic rounding is not the remedy. Round-to-nearest is biased, and bias is what compounds through a recurrence, so stochastic rounding ( Gupta et al., 2015 ) is the standard fix and the one the Nemotron 3 line ships for its SSM cache ( NVIDIA, 2026 ) . It costs 6.71 6.71 nats on top of yoked INT4 ( t = 41.1 t=41.1 ) and 5.77 5.77 on top of self-scaled INT4 ( t = 17.2 t=17.2 ), falling to 0.62 0.62 at INT8 ( t = 10.5 t=10.5 ). Removing the bias makes each step’s error larger— 2 \sqrt{2} in RMS, 1.42 × 1.42\times measured on the states—and a recurrence amplifies magnitude, not sign. Against exposure it holds all three policies between 9.7 9.7 and 11.2 11.2 nats out to 32K, worse at every checkpoint than clearing the state (Appendix D ). Three ways of spending the same bits. Each of the following gives the quantizer more information than uniform group-wise scaling does, after the outlier-aware designs that work on weights, activations and the KV cache ( Lin et al., 2024 ; Hooper et al., 2024 ) , and each is beaten by it. • Outlier-frequency channel targeting / exact sparse escape. Giving extra bits to the most frequently-overflowing channels, or storing overflowing elements exactly, does not beat a random channel subset or uniform allocation—locating outliers is not containing the feedback. • Dynamic → \to static and static → \to dynamic hybrids. A hybrid that runs dynamic early and static late does beat both pure policies, because the late static caps the runaway. It still loses to group-wise ( t = − 14.2 t=-14.2 ). • Capped dynamic scaling. Beats static, loses to group-wise ( t = − 10.0 t=-10.0 ). Its exact-escape variant adds nothing (Table 1 ): the cap is what helps, not the escape. A temporal grid-churn account does not survive matched controls either. Uniform group-wise scaling beats all three. Persistent group-wise INT4 is the least-damaging policy at every GDN model and horizon, at a lower modeled bit rate than uniform INT5. It beats persistent static INT4 by t = − 25 t=-25 to − 29 -29 at 0.8B and t = − 12 t=-12 at 2B, and it beats each design above by t = − 10 t=-10 to − 19 -19 (Table 1 ). Static and group-wise both remove the feedback edge and differ only in how many scales they spend on the channel axis, whereas every design above spends its extra information on finding outliers instead. This is the least damaging uniform policy on these models, and we did not invent any part of it. A caution for practitioners. Even the best policy is far from lossless. At H = 2048 H=2048 uniform group-wise INT4 leaves natural-text perplexity at 7.8 × 7.8\times the unquantized model on 0.8B and 8.6 × 8.6\times on 2B, and the best leak-free allocation still costs 4.9 × 4.9\times and 7.4 × 7.4\times . Both pure INT4 policies are worse here than clearing the state altogether, so none of these options is usable. Quantization that preserves perfect NIAH recall can still severely damage general language-modeling quality : recall of a single planted fact is a far weaker probe of state fidelity than natural continuation. Figure 4: Per-layer allocation. (a) Quantizing one layer at a time, plotted at the true layer index; gaps are attention rather than linear-attention layers. (b) Rate–distortion. The connected series are an in-sample sweep, optimistic in level because the protected layers were chosen on the articles they are scored on. The star re-measures the same 4.0-bit policy under the leak-free protocol of Table 4 , and that gap is why the curves sit below the table. Does per-layer mixed precision help? A leak-free test. Per-layer mixed precision is the natural refinement, because single-layer sensitivity is strongly concentrated. Quantizing one layer at a time to INT4, the first GDN layer alone accounts for 63 63 – 78 % 78\% of the summed single-layer damage at H = 2048 H=2048 (Figure 4 a). The obvious move is to protect a few layers at high precision and quantize the rest aggressively. We test that under a leak-free protocol, with calibration, selection, and test articles disjoint by title hash (6, 15, and 18 articles). Layer selection runs under the deployment quantizer, persistent group-wise, by marginal rescue from an all-INT2 baseline, and every reported number is on the held-out test articles (Table 4 , Figure 4 b). The positive finding. Extreme allocation—top-3 layers at INT8, the rest at INT2, averaging 4.0 bits—is a genuine Pareto improvement over uniform group-wise at a matched budget, beating uniform INT3 at the same 4.0 bits by t = − 12.8 t=-12.8 at 0.8B. It also beats uniform INT4 at a 20% lower rate, though that higher-rate margin attenuates with model scale, from t = − 10.3 t=-10.3 at 0.8B to t = − 2.2 t=-2.2 at 2B. Choosing the right layers is what does the work: the rescue-selected allocation beats random, inverse, and reconstruction-MSE-ranked allocations by t = − 17 t=-17 to − 22 -22 . The deflationary one. The sensitive layers are simply the first layers. Rescue selection, a matched-budget knapsack optimizer, and a trivial “protect the first three layers” baseline return numerically identical results, not merely similar ones (Table 4 ). No learned or search-based allocation adds anything over the trivial heuristic.
