The ordering is monotone at both scales, yet the best policy looks lossless at h ≤ 512 h\leq 512 and has failed on a third of articles by h = 2048 h=2048 . 9 How long is a quantized state safe? Excess NLL averages over a window and hides when a policy first breaks, so we add a reliability view. Feeding the FP and a quantized model the same tokens, we record the first step at which the quantized model flips a next-token argmax that FP had predicted with a top-2 logit margin above 8. That first-passage failure time τ \tau is measured on 30 held-out articles up to H = 8 H=8 K, right-censored at article length. The survival curve Pr ⁡ ( τ > h ) \Pr(\tau>h) (Figure 5 ) orders the policies monotonically at every horizon, and at every FP-confidence threshold (Appendix F ): first-layer-protected group-wise, then group-wise, then static and dynamic together. At H = 2048 H=2048 , protected group-wise leaves 19 of 30 articles confident-token-faithful, group-wise 5 of 30, and the two pure policies none. There is no strategy reversal here. The best policy short is the best policy long, so on this metric short evaluation does not select the wrong policy, unlike the crossover of § 7 . But short evaluation badly underestimates risk. The deployment-preferred policy looks essentially lossless at short horizon, failing on 1 of 30 articles by H = 512 H=512 . By H = 2048 H=2048 it has failed on 11 of 30, and those long-horizon failures have no short-horizon precursor. It replicates at 2B: 0 of 30 by H = 512 H=512 , 12 of 30 by H = 2048 H=2048 . Failure horizons cannot be extrapolated from short traces either: a constant- or power-law-hazard fit to the first 256 steps mis-predicts survival at H = 2048 H=2048 by well over an octave, because the good policy has no short-window events to fit. Evaluating recurrent-state quantization at short length is hazardous not because it ranks policies wrongly, but because it certifies a policy as safe long before its failures appear. 10 Discussion and conclusion What generalizes. A single-architecture result would not be worth much, so it matters that the exposure interaction (§ 7 ) and the failure frontier both replicate across GDN (0.8B, 2B) and Mamba-2 (1.3B), the frontier sitting about twice as far out on the SSM. Group-wise dominance does not: it holds at both GDN scales and fails on Mamba-2 (Table 2 ). Concurrent work approaches low-precision recurrent inference by other routes—decay-aware mixed precision applied to the state itself ( Zhang et al., 2026 ) , and a per-element floating-point format applied to weights and activations with the state left in high precision ( Kozyrev and Maiboroda, 2026 ) —neither of which we compare against here. Severity varies with architecture while the functional interaction does not, so the interaction belongs to quantized recurrent-state decoding and not to the delta rule. One principle, four findings. The positive results are one idea seen four ways: a persistent scale eliminates the feedback edge, a calibrated ceiling bounds it, periodic reset interrupts it, and a higher bit-width merely delays the loop. That every outlier-locating policy failed is the same principle read backwards. What we would tell a practitioner. Prefer any persistently calibrated scale over per-token dynamic scaling, check group-wise against plain static on the target architecture rather than assuming group-wise wins, protect the first recurrent layer, and expect little from learned allocation beyond that. The point we would most want carried forward is the reporting one: a bit-width certified at 512 steps says little about 4K and nothing about 32K, and the horizon is where low-bit recurrent-state inference actually breaks. Limitations Measurement. We simulate quantization rather than implement a packed kernel, so bit rates are modeled and we report no latency or throughput. The best policy still leaves perplexity at 7.8 × 7.8\times (0.8B) and 8.6 × 8.6\times (2B) the unquantized model at H = 2048 H=2048 . We run no head-to-head against architecture-specific quantizers (Q-Mamba, Quamba2, DAMP), which differ in both what they quantize and at what rate, and make no systems claim. Scope and mechanism. Two architectures and three model sizes, all below 3B; the first-layer-protection advantage already shrinks from 0.8B to 2B, so we cannot say whether it survives at deployment scale. Scale-yoking identifies the feedback as the cause of the numerical runaway but recovers only part of the functional loss, and we do not identify the remainder; § 5 records the countervailing evidence and the run-to-run instability of the norm itself. Ethics statement This work is an empirical analysis of numerical stability in quantized inference. It uses publicly released model checkpoints and the public WikiText-103 corpus, introduces no new data collection, and involves no human subjects or personally identifying information. The synthetic recall probes are generated from fictional entities. The practical effect of the findings, if any, is to make low-bit long-context inference more reliable and to warn against a specific evaluation practice (certifying a quantizer at short decode length) that can overstate deployed reliability. We see no direct dual-use concern beyond those already attached to efficient LLM inference generally. Reproducibility All experiments use public model checkpoints and the WikiText-103 corpus, and every run reported here fits on a single RTX 3090. Code, result files and the project page are at https://avalon-s.github.io/dynamic-scaling-fails/ . The release carries the fake-quantization, calibration and evaluation code, the article-disjoint calibration/selection/test splits by title hash, the result file behind every number reported here, the plotting scripts that build every figure directly from those files, and the per-run provenance (article IDs, quantizer, group size, model and data revision). GDN runs are bit-identical between independent executions: re-running the long-horizon sweep of Appendix E from scratch reproduced all 35 per-document excess-NLL values to the last digit. The Mamba-2 runtime is not deterministic, and repeating the same configuration moves a single-document loss by a few hundredths of a nat, so Mamba numbers should be read as reproducible in distribution rather than exactly. State norms reproduce far less well than losses, because a runaway amplifies whatever differs between runs: across three executions the dynamic-INT4 norm at H = 2048 H=2048 ranges from 38.9 38.9 to 42.3 42.3 while the corresponding excess NLL moves by 0.4 % 0.4\% .
